utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Madam Registrar, please have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is the interpretation booth ready and rested after the hard work of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Blaskic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLASKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you well, Mr. Blaskic? The detention conditions are convenient? Did you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard you. I am very well and everything is fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Can everyone hear me? The Office of the Prosecutor, the Defence? Very well. Yes, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I can hear you, your Honour, although I do not see a transcript on the video monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well yes, you are right, everything is fine except that. Before beginning, perhaps we have to correct this problem with the transcript. Mr. Dubuisson, Mme Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is it coming? No. Do you think it will come in a second or two? It is not correct for the judges to sit at the bench. We will suspend the hearing for five minutes; you must let us know when everything is operative. We will rise for five minutes. (10.10 am) (A short break) (10.15 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Madam Registrar, is everything functioning now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. Mr. Prosecutor, Mr. Kehoe, good morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, good morning Mr. President, your Honours. The Prosecutor would call Edin Beso. If I can ask the assistance of the usher to escort Mr. Beso in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: While he is arriving, your Honour, a housekeeping matter. The Tribunal directed the Defence to produce the entire statement of Mr. Remi Landry in yesterday's session and I have it. I will tender it to the Registrar. For the record, it is 12 pages in length and it is tendered subject to the objections previously noted by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we have admitted it as evidence in its totality; is that not so, Mr. Harmon? There is no objection in that regard. We just need the translation, Mme Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that is why I am asking for the French translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Fine, I am sure we will be able to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, I would remind you of that. Mr. Kehoe, Mr. Edin Beso, you have planned two and a half hours for him; is that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, that is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. I think the usher has gone to bring him in. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, will you first tell me whether you can hear me, Mr. Beso? Just a moment. Can you hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you tell me who you are, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Edin Beso; I was born on 23rd May 1971.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, that is sufficient for the moment. You will be giving those answers to the Prosecutor. I would like to ask you to read the declaration that the usher has just given to you, the document you are holding in your right hand. Can you read it, please, in your language? EDIN BESO (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Beso. You may be seated now. Mr. Beso, you are addressing the International Criminal Tribunal. You have been cited as a witness by the Prosecutor who will question you first. After that, you will be cross-examined by the Defence. You must speak without any fear, you must have no fear; you are talking to judges and that is what the judges wanted to tell you before we begin. Mr. Prosecutor, it is your witness; you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Beso, after introducing yourself, you were giving us your date of birth. What is your date of birth, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 23rd May 1971. I was born in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For most of your life, in what municipality did you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of my life I lived in the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In what part of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For some time I lived in the old part of Vitez which is called Old Vitez, Stari Vitez. From 1982 onwards, I lived in the part of Vitez called Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, are you a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In Rijeka, was that a mixed neighbourhood or was it mostly a Muslim neighbourhood or mostly a Croat neighbourhood? Tell the judges what kind of neighbourhood Rijeka was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rijeka was a mixed neighbourhood. There were quite a few people living there, Croats, Serbs, Muslims and nearby, there was also a gypsy settlement, so it was a mixed neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, if you can look to your left on the easel, Mr. President and your Honours, once again on the easel is a photograph, a copy of Prosecutor's exhibit 56 and I believe, in consultation with Mme Fauveau, this is 56B.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, 56B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso and Mr. President, with the court's permission, if you could take the pink marker that is to your left and if you could go up to the photograph and circle your house in Rijeka. May I approach, Mr. President, as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Rijeka. That is where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. You have marked that with the pink; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you could now take the green and just basically give the general outline of the Rijeka area. It does not have to be exact; just give us some rough approximation of where Rijeka is. Could you fill that in for us, just put a circle around it; make it a little darker so the court can see it? That is good.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps it is not very accurate, but that is about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That would be a rough approximation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you can just step back, using the pointer, can you point to the area known as Kruscica on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You can have a seat again, thank you. Mr. Beso, once again, what year did your family move to the house in Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, when you were living in the former Yugoslavia, was there an obligation to serve in the Yugoslav People's Army when you reached a certain age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not getting a translation through here. What was the obligation of every man to serve in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an obligation if the man was healthy, when he received call-up papers, when he was registered, then he would be sent to a certain place in the former Yugoslavia where he would do his military service for a year, 12 months to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you serve in the JNA, Mr. Beso?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When did you begin your service and when did you end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went into the Jugoslav People's Army on 18th March 1990 and I came back on 8th March 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was your experience of going into the JNA similar to other healthy men in the Vitez area during the 1990s and before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you got to the Yugoslav People's Army, did you go through training when you first came into the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went through training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell the court about the training you received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went for training in the town of Senta in Vojvodina near Subotica. When I came to the barracks we were taken in, of course,, we received uniforms and everything else that we needed and then we had a certain period of adjusting to life in the barracks. Then basic military training started, the usual routine for soldiers like saluting officers. I was in the technical services, in the mechanical units of the infantry, so I did not have proper infantry training, it was very short, five or six days. After that, we had training in classrooms, how to repair rifles, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did soldiers in the infantry and the artillery sections have additional training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, their training was longer. My training was two months and 22 days. Their training was six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, after you finished your training, what assignment did you have in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I went to Macedonia to the town of Bitolj where I worked on the overhaul and repair of infantry arms. I stayed there until the very end of my military service, 8th March, when I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you say you went home, Mr. Beso, did you come back to Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you came back to Rijeka in 1991, Mr. Beso, what did you do? Did you get involved in politics, did you get involved in government, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not interested in politics. I simply went on with my pre-army life. Naturally I did not have a job; I had completed school before that, so I worked a bit at home. I did a bit of agriculture work, I would go out regularly, to cafes in Vitez, to Travnik, to Novi Travnik, Busovaca, so that is how I spent my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you involved in sporting activities as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for a certain period of time, even before I went to the army, in the town soccer club of Vitez. I started playing soccer, but after an injury, I had to leave football, so then I played a bit of basketball and then again I went back to soccer, but all of that was very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, tell the court a little bit about your own personal circumstances living in Rijeka. Who did you live with; who lived in the same house with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My parents were divorced. My father went on living in Sarajevo where we all lived until then. I was a very small child when I returned to Vitez with my mother and my brother. We lived in Stari Vitez for four years and then we came to Rijeka where my father built a house for us. We lived there on the money that my father sent in regularly; my brother and I received an education, my mother was not employed anywhere, and when we finished school and when my brother came back from the JNA, he got a job in the mine in Zenica where he worked, so our life became a bit easier. That was it, but also nearby there were two houses of our relatives; my aunt lived in one of these houses. My uncle died before the war, I do not know which year, and then also in the neighbourhood was another aunt of mine, my paternal uncle's wife, but my paternal uncle had been killed in a bicycle accident before the war, but we were all very close. Just before the war, my mother's mother came to visit us, but she was an invalid, so she went on living with us until she died. My aunt went to Switzerland just before the war, so she also left us her house and the other facilities she had. My aunt had a cow, so we continued feeding her cow, so that is the way it was, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Beso, at the outbreak of the war, you were living in the same house with your brother, your mother and your grandmother; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me take you to 1992 when the war broke out. When the war broke out, Mr. Beso, did you join the Armija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in a special situation; I was younger than my brother. My brother immediately joined the Territorial Defence as it was then called. I continued to help out at home. My granny was disabled, so I stayed there with her and my mother and then after that, I joined the BH-Army, but I cannot remember on what date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Was it some time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What job did you have when you joined the BH-Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked the command to give me an assignment which would not keep me away from home a lot, because I had many things to do at home and it was only natural that I had to take care of that. In our country in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when the war broke out, the television lines were mostly under the control of the Bosnian Serbs, so from Bosnia to -- from Rijeka to Kruscica, a relay station was made so that Bosnian television from Sarajevo could be seen. My superiors gave me orders to secure that relay station, so I would work there every now and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were working at the TV station, did you come back and forth and stay at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was nearby, so I would go on bicycle; it was not very far away. I would spend a day there and then a day at home, so I would alternate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, let me direct your attention to the morning of 16th April 1993, the morning the war broke out in Vitez. Do you remember that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In your own words, Mr. Beso, tell the judges what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 16th April 1993 in the early morning hours, my mother woke me up, saying that detonations and shooting could be heard. I went out of the house. Dawn had just broken, and detonations and shooting could be heard from all over. I did not know what was going on, but the situation was strange; you could feel war in the air. I knew that war had broken out. I did not know what to do. The house did not have a cellar, and I told my mother that I would take her and my grandmother to the house next door where there was a cellar and they should stay there until we decided what we should do later. When I took them over to the house next door -- it was right next door, it was owned by Sifet Adilovic. He was temporarily employed in Switzerland and two girls from Zenica lived in his house. They took care of his house, I do not know why they were there. When I took my mother and my granny there, my grandmother was disabled, as I said, so I went back to our home to get her the medicine that she used to take regularly. At one point in time when I was going back to Sifet Adilovic's house, about 50 metres away along the road, I saw a few soldiers in camouflage uniforms who were taking civilians, men, along with them. I recognised my Muslim neighbours, but I did not know where they were going. When I brought in the medicine, my mother told me that I should feed the cow. Naturally I was afraid, but I had to do it. I went back to the house again, I took the keys to the stable and the garage where the cattlefeed was. I climbed on the stables to get some hay for the cow; that is probably when the HVO noticed me. As I was going down from the second floor of the stables, a few members came in, they were all my neighbours, they were wearing uniforms. They said, "Hands up", and they said I should lean against the wall. They searched me, they wanted to know whether I had any weapons, they searched the stables and the garage all over and they told me to change and they told me that I was their prisoner. From there they took me to the veterinary station that was in Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for one moment, Mr. Beso. The soldiers that you saw that arrested you, you said that you recognised them, that they were your neighbours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who were these men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of them was Rajko Matkovic. I knew him for a certain period of time; he was the oldest one of them all. Then there was Krunoslav Bonic, who we used to call Kico, then Karin Goran and another young man; I knew him but I cannot remember his name. He was also from Rijeka. They were all wearing uniforms and they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you say they were wearing uniforms, what type of uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms with HVO patches on their sleeves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, you said that when you first came out of your house, you saw soldiers taking men out of Vares houses in your neighbourhood; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you step up to the map and with the pointer just point to the line of houses for the court where these men were being arrested from. Mr. Beso, when you point to it, could you just hold the pointer to the area for one moment so the camera can focus in on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is this series of houses (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were all of those houses inhabited by Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were mixed. There were Muslim houses, Croat houses, there was a Serb house on the other side. There were two Muslim houses, then Croat houses then Muslim houses here, so it was all mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were all the men that were being arrested Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, have a seat, please. Mr. Beso, you said that after you were arrested, you were taken to the veterinary station.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might show you a -- Mme Fauveau, exhibit 33, with the assistance of the usher and if we could ask for the ELMO to be put on, I would just like to show you a series of photographs. Mr. Usher, I will be looking at the photographs towards the back of that exhibit, PH225 and PH226. I am sorry, Cedric, I think they were the back photographs. Mr. Beso, looking at the photograph that is on the monitor, do you recognise that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That is the veterinary station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were brought to the veterinary station, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to the basement of the veterinary station. When I came, the basement was full of Muslims. I do not know exactly how many there were. All of them lived in Rijeka in the Sofa and Podsofa neighbourhood, so I knew all of them because they were neighbours of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you see the entrance on that photograph that you went into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you just point on the ELMO with it, sir, with the pointer if you could?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For the record, you are pointing to the doorway on the right side of the photograph; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could just put the other photograph on the ELMO quickly? What does that photograph depict, Mr. Beso?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is also the house where the veterinary station was and where we were, that is we, the prisoners from Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is simply the other side of the same building in the photograph that we just saw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. Mr. President, I would just ask that the usher not put the exhibit back together again because we are going to be using a couple of photographs later on in the testimony. Mr. Beso, tell us about the conditions in the basement of the veterinary station.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions were poor. It was cold, it was a dark room; the walls were very damp, they were wet even. We were not allowed to go out for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were there many other men in the basement with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only we the Muslims who had been brought there from their homes. We were guarded, there were guards all around the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were all these guards members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, because they were all our Croat neighbours. They had insignia, rifles, uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell the judges about what happened to you when you were being kept in the basement of the veterinary station. Were you taken anywhere after a period of time in the station? Tell the court what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there for a certain period of time, I do not know exactly for how long. We would get some food, canned fish, that was too little, we did not get any cigarettes, only if people had taken something from their homes. Later on they would allow Muslim women to bring us food from their homes, some clothes, blankets. I do not know exactly when, but they started taking us out to dig trenches. I was chosen to go along with one of the groups. They mostly included younger people. We were taken to the hill of Sofa, where we dug trenches facing the village of Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, who took you out to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken out to dig trenches, I mean the group that I was in, by Kico Bonic, and another soldier too was there too, but I do not know exactly who.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But were they HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could ask the witness to approach the overhead again, 56, and if I can approach as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Defence may approach as well if they wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, you told us previously that the area circled in green is Rijeka and that the area that is moving up to the right of the green is Kruscica. You just mentioned an area that you call Sofa. Could you take the pointer again and just step back and just hold it on there to the area that you call Sofa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just hold it there for one moment. Okay, sir. You said that you were digging trenches in that area; can you just with the orange marker mark the area that you were digging trenches in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were first digging trenches somewhere around here; these were individual trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What do you mean by individual trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance they were not in a single part, we did not have to interlink them, we did not have to do any extra digging. These were simply trenches meant to have individual soldiers in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you mark that a little heavier so the court can see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is where we were first digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that the line where you were first digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and then later on we were taken to the gypsy neighbourhood to dig there, that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was there a reason that you were taken to the gypsy neighbourhood to dig trenches later on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but rumour had it that HVO members believed that the BH-Army was stationed in the gypsy neighbourhood, but since they realised that they were not there, they took us to Ciglane facing the Kruscica village to dig trenches over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did an HVO commander come on the scene to take you up there to dig those other trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we were digging at the first place, a commander came and he was very angry and he was shouting at his soldier why we were digging trenches there; why did we not dig them closer to Kruscica? Then, about half an hour later, they took us to this other place. As we were digging, they were shooting over our heads towards the Kruscica village and we were out there in the open and we were digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who was shooting over your heads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Karin Goran, also a person from Rijeka, his surname is Males; I cannot remember his first name. Then the local Serbs who lived in Sofa, they also belonged to the HVO, they were also shooting towards Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: These were HVO soldiers shooting over your head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So for the sake of clarity, this is the first place you were digging trenches, I put the number 1; and this was the second place; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you could have a seat again and I will go back to the podium, your Honour. Mr. Beso, how long did you dig trenches towards Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but we were taken there in the morning and we were brought back to the veterinary station late in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many men were out there digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about ten of us in the group, I do not know exactly, ten or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, you said that late in the evening you were brought back to the veterinarian station. Did you go back to the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then a second group was taken there to dig. When we came back, we were given something to eat. I do not know exactly how much more time we spent there and then again it was my turn and I was taken to dig trenches in another place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where was the next place you were taken to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the village of Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could request the assistance of the usher to put up what is now, I believe, a copy of exhibit 50, and I believe at this point we are on 50B. If we could just put this over the other one, that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mme Fauveau, it is a copy of which photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is a copy of 50 and this is document 50B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, tell us about going to Pirici. What road did you follow and how did you get there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were in the veterinary station and when we were taken out again we were mostly young men. In front of the station, a white Mercedes van was parked. We climbed into it and we were taken along the road passing Rijeka, the railway station --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I do not have the translation. Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we reached Pirici, actually there were two groups, one group got off at Zume and the second group that I belonged to was taken to Pirici. Then we continued working, digging; we were guarded by HVO members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did HVO members take you from the veterinary station out to Pirici as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, if we could turn our attention to the overhead that is on the easel which is 50B, and again, Mr. President, if I may approach, and if you could step up also. Mr. Beso, this is a photograph that has been received in evidence. Is the area that you came to dig trenches in Pirici depicted on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the village of Pirici. This is where we were brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you could just hold the pointer there for one moment so the camera can see it. When you were taken there, sir, were you forced to dig trenches there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again using the orange marker on 50B, could you circle the approximate area where you were digging trenches in the Pirici area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were digging in several areas. I do not know exactly, but around here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Without being exact, those are the approximate areas that you were digging trenches; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, your Honours, there are three orange lines written by the witness on Prosecutor's exhibit 50B. Mr. Beso, if you could have a seat? Your Honour, I will go back to the podium. Mr. Beso, when you got to Pirici to dig trenches, tell the judges what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got there, we were divided up into smaller groups, so the soldiers took us group by group to dig. I do not know exactly for how long we were digging, but we were tired, we had hardly any rest at all, and at one point, while we were digging the trenches, shooting was suddenly heard between the army and the HVO, because we were in between the lines. The lines had not really been formed properly yet, so that a colleague of mine who was captured with me and detained was wounded in the chest on that occasion and he fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Salih Sadibasic. He also used to live in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell us about how he was shot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not killed, he was wounded in the chest. When he was taken away, HVO members gave him first aid, they bandaged his wound and transferred him to the hospital in Travnik where he recovered. We continued the digging, and we had taken shelter for a while from the fire, but we could not stay there; we were ordered to continue digging. I do not know exactly for how long this went on. Then they told us to take all our tools, the tools we had been using for the digging, and to go to a house where we would be given something to eat. When we got there, we left our tools aside. We were very tired, so we sat down straight away on the grass. We were given food. Again there were tins, canned fish, some bread. I do not know exactly what it was, some kind of cabbage stew, and we ate it. While eating, we were watched by HVO members who were guarding us, and one of the detainees who was living in Vitez. I know him from before, he was a bit sickly, something mentally, I do not know exactly what it was. Later, talking amongst ourselves, we detainees came to the conclusion that he was so shocked by Salih's injury, he was frightened out of his wits. He looked at the HVO members standing next to us and he noticed that one of them had carelessly left his rifle. He jumped up, took the rifle and he wanted to cock it, but I think he did not know how to use a weapon, and he started running towards the lines held by the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The HVO members caught up with him, and some of them did not have their weapons on them. They took tools, the implements we had been using, a shovel and a pick, and they started hitting him with these implements. We were close by but we did not dare do anything. We just sat there, because we were threatened and they guarded us with arms, and I saw this man's blood flowing. His head was split, his skull, but he was still on his feet. They snatched away the gun and continued beating him. He started staggering, but he was a strongly-built man, a tall young man. Then suddenly one of the people, I do not know exactly who he was, he had a long leather jacket on him, an elderly man, he took a pistol, I saw well the model; it was a Crvena Zastava 7.62 millimetre. He fired into his stomach, but he was still on his feet. Then the HVO members created a kind of mess; they did not seem to be aware what was happening, there was a big group of them. I did not know all of them well, because I did not go to those parts very often. They called each other by Vares names and then another one came up, also an HVO member, and he killed this man with a burst of fire from a Kalasnjikov and he fell there. We were ordered to move him from there, just to put him next to a wall and they would see later what they would do with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, what was the name of the man that was murdered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ibrakovic. We called him Jusa. I am not sure whether his first name was Jusuf but he was his name was Ibrakovic, and we called him Jusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you hear the names of any HVO soldiers that were there at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, while we were digging trenches, the guards who were there watching us, they probably thought that we were not listening, that we were busy working, so I heard that Slavko Papic was some kind of a commander there in that part. Later, after this killing, they said that Dragan should not have done this and he should have done that, as if Dragan Papic had actually killed Jusuf, but there were quite a number of them there; I did not know all of them. There was a totally unknown man. He had a very good uniform on him, a better quality, much better quality than the others, and he was one of the group. What actually happened after that, we were ordered to lie on the ground on the road leading to Ahmici and that we simply must not move until they decided what to do with us. Then again, later, a soldier came and told us to take our tools and to continue with the digging. As we were moving towards a burnt-down house to dig, this Slavko Papic -- he was an older man, a commander -- said that they needed to kill another one because they were afraid that we might do something. He looked at prisoner Amir Koco. We again resumed digging until late into the night the shooting calmed down, so that we continued digging with some relief. I was in great fear, so that all these events seemed like eternity to me, and it was night already. I remember it was dark, it must have been late. They took us to a cellar. I could not see very well in the dark, but there were the remains of a house that had burned down and there was just the cellar and we were put up there. It was a cellar, there was nothing there. There was some kind of shelf; probably the former owner had kept apples or potatoes there, so they locked us up there; we were dirty from the earth. We could not even talk, we were so terrified, and while there was -- while they were locking us up, one of the members said, "if I hear a sound from you" -- he said he would throw a hand grenade through the window, which is like a big bomb. Perhaps we dozed off after that, but before that, while I was still digging, some HVO members would come up to us as we were guided up into groups. They would offer us cigarettes, and they told us not to be so scared, but I did not trust anyone. I was so scared; I think among all my friends I was frightened most. Then a young man came up to me. He had a uniform and a rifle. He was staring at me while I was digging while another one was guarding me. He told me, "Do not expose yourself so much; bend down while you are digging." I just looked at him, I did not dare talk to him, I did not know who he was. He had a different accent; he did not speak like the rest of us from Vitez. He had a typical kind of accent. I do not know exactly where he was from. He told me he was from Zagreb. Whether he was or not, I do not know. Then later he told some people that he was from Kotor Varos, which is a town in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then somehow we started talking about insignificant things. We did not talk about the war at all. We spoke about music, the kind of music I listen to, what he liked to listen to, which sport he liked and that sort of thing from our youth. That very morning, this same soldier came to the cellar where we were locked up and he told us to follow him. We were taken from Pirici to the cinema in Vitez, and we were handed over there. When we got to the cinema, I saw a lot of captured Muslims there. I saw several members wearing uniforms who had white belts, and had the insignia of the military police. We were handed over to Anto Kovac, whom we all called Zabac. He took us over and the military police members took us up in the cinema. The hall itself was full, the boiler room was full and there were some offices upstairs, they were all full, full of captured Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if you consider it to be convenient, perhaps we could break now and continue at 11.45. Does that suit you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will have a break and resume work at 11.45. (11.25 am) (A short break). (11.45 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The session is continued, please bring in the accused. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Beso, Ibrakovic Jusa, the man that was murdered up in Pirici, was he a Muslim as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am sorry, let me repeat that question and answer. The man that was murdered up in Pirici, Ibrakovic Jusa, was he a Muslim as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, just before the break, you told the court that you were taken from Pirici to the cinema; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission and with the assistance of the usher, I would like to move to Prosecutor's exhibit 33 and the photographs that we have in 33 are PH197, PH198 and PH203.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is for the same purpose, for expediting the proceedings. Perhaps we could ask the Registrar to see what exhibits will be mentioned in advance, so that we know in advance what are the photographs or the exhibits that will be discussed, if this is possible. Is that convenient to you, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President, and Mme Fauveau and I did discuss that at the break, that we were going to move into those photographs and as a result she had those photographs on top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. My colleague says the same goes for the Defence too, of course. Please, try to prepare in advance all the exhibits you can. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. Mr. Beso, the photograph that is now on the ELMO, PH197, do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the cinema, the cinema in Vitez. Before it was called Aradnis Kuravesita, the workers' university of Mosa Pijade in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could just move to photograph PH198 and then after that PH203. Is that likewise a photograph of a different angle of the cinema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That is where the exit was from the cinema hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The last photograph, PH203. How about that photograph, Mr. Beso? Is that another angle of the cinema from the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This was the entrance to the cinema hall and also to the other facilities there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was that the door that you were brought in when you were brought to the cinema after you were taken from digging trenches in Pirici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am not going to use the ELMO any more, Mr. Usher, so we can move on from these photographs. Going back, Mr. Beso, tell us about what happened to you when you were taken to the cinema.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived in the cinema, as I said, we were taken over by Anto Kovac; his nickname was Zabac. He was some kind of commander in the military police. Then the policemen put us in the rooms where there was room, because the place was crowded. I was in an office on the first floor which was crowded. When the other prisoners saw me, saw me all grimy and dirty from the earth, my jacket and my trousers. They asked me where I had been and I told them that I had been digging trenches. They told me, "People go to dig trenches from here too."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where did they tell you that people were being taken to dig trenches from the cinema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They told me that they were taken to Krcevine, towards Kuber, Krizanveve Kuce, the village of Jardol. I cannot remember whether they mentioned any other places too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Beso. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we were there, I noticed that the Muslim prisoners were allowed to receive visitors. Their relatives would come in, their wives, their mothers, their sisters. They would bring them food, also clothes that people needed, so my family also heard about this, that I had been moved there, and a relative of mine brought me some clothes, coffee, food, cigarettes, so I thought things would be better for me there. I thought that I would not have to go dig trenches anywhere else any more. I got new clothes, so I was not the way I had been before that. I cannot remember the exact date, but I was chosen once again to go and dig trenches in the village of Krcevine near Vitez. A group of us was sent, of younger men, again, naturally. We dug in a forest facing the village of Krcevine. We did whatever had to be done in order to set up a frontline there too. We worked very hard. We would get very little rest. We ate the leftovers from the soldiers who were on the frontline. We were guarded all the time. In the forest that I mentioned, we dug holes and then we would dig trenches to connect them. From the nearby village we would bring in timber boards that were made of beechwood; they were very heavy. Then we would cover the holes, put nylon over them and thus make underground shelter. So every soldier who was there was giving us instructions, what kind of shelter he would like to have and how we should dig this. From that forest to a lone house that stood there, we dug a big trench. This was a clearing, so it was not safe for them to move there. At one moment, while we were carrying boards and coming back, this was in daylight, there was non-stop shooting, so we were actually exposed to this crossfire. At one point, a schoolfriend of mine, with whom I had spent a lot of time -- he was also a Muslim, Gadjun Amir -- he was also a prisoner; he lived in the part of Vitez which was called Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is he also a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When the shooting started, I was standing near him, also another colleague of ours, Almas Zuljevic, another Muslim who was also a prisoner, who was standing nearby too -- we were out there working -- he was hit in the neck, so he fell there on the meadow. I was lost during those very first moments, I did not know what we were supposed to do, so we lay on the ground too. Then somehow with the help of the members of the HVO, we evacuated Amir from there. We moved him behind a house where a soldier gave us you his first aid bag, so we bandaged his neck. He was hit very badly in a bad place. We tried to carry him to a car, to a vehicle, because we were told that he would be taken to a hospital. As we were carrying him there, we saw that he was very weak, he was very dark. We put him down and another prisoner took his tongue out of his mouth because he was suffocating. He only opened his eyes, he briefly looked at us. He just managed to say, "Say hello to my mother for me", and he did not say anything else. He passed away then. Again we were taken back to dig trenches; he was dragged away from there. Later I found out that he was buried in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, I know that you do not have a recollection of exact dates, but do you know approximately how long after 16th April this killing of Almir Gadjun took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, that was the greatest problem I had, to know which day was which, so approximately -- I do not know, about ten or fifteen days later. I cannot tell exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were taken out to Krcevine, how many men were taken out with you to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A group that was pretty big, 12 or 15 people. While we were digging, there were no other incidents, only Almir was killed. Some HVO members threatened us; they said we had to work and it was a good thing for them while we had them there and we would really be in trouble if the Jokeri came, and we did not know who the Jokeri were at that time. I even saw some of my schoolfriends up there who were also members of the HVO. When they saw me, they were surprised too; how come that I had been detained? They asked me if I was hungry, whether I needed anything. They gave me cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, you said that you were threatened by members of the HVO regarding the Jokeri. Did they mention the Vitezovi as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not, that group with which I was. They just said, "It will be very difficult for you when the Jokeri come. It is better for you to finish as soon as possible. The sooner you finish, the better for you." We spent a lot of time there digging. We did not really have any rest. We were digging and digging, day and night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were the soldiers that were guarding you in Sofa, Pirici and Krcevine all members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of them. Only while we were digging at Sofa, I saw the Serbs who lived there too; they were not wearing uniforms. They were wearing civilian clothes, but they had rifles in their hands. They were armed but they were not wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At any time while you were digging trenches, were you guarded by members of the Jokeri or of the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I never had the opportunity of seeing them while I was digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After Gadjun Almir was killed and you said you continued to dig, how much longer did you continue to dig before you were brought back to the cinema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We continued to dig that day, that night, and the next day, and then we were replaced by other prisoners, and we were driven back to where we had been before, the cinema in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What happened when you got back to the cinema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came back to the cinema, we were all sort of lost. Things continued as before; people were taken to dig trenches all the time. I was not taken anywhere any more. I know that some people were being brought in and others were being taken away. At one point in time, some journalists arrived. I do not know where they were from. They filmed us, a lady journalist; she spoke English. She was looking at me and she told the cameraman to film me because I had dirt all over me, earth, and he did that. Once while we were there one evening, I heard some doors slam and I heard some names being read out, and the next morning, I found out that prominent Muslims, engineers, professors, workers who had worked in Slobodan Princip Selo factory at responsible posts, they were all taken away. At that point, I did not know why this was done. The Red Cross arrived that day. They took down all our names, they registered us, they gave us some kind of cards. Then it was different. I did not say that while we were at the cinema, we were regularly fed by the HVO members. The food that was given to us consisted of a tin and a quarter of a bread loaf. After that, they were brought in all the time and once when a visitor came to see me some of my friends and relatives came in, girls, and they were telling me about the Croats expelling people from their houses and that they did not know what to do. Before that, I had heard about this too. I knew that everything was being done by force and that you were not supposed to offer any kind of resistance. I told them to wait, because we had already heard some stories that we would be released, and another girl, a relative, told me that there were a lot of women in our house because they had been driven out of their own homes. I did not know what to tell them then. I just said, "If you want to, you can leave, but if you want to, you can wait until they release me." I always kept thinking of my mother and my grandmother, who was disabled, and I knew that it was difficult to evacuate them towards Zenica and Travnik. One day again the Red Cross had arrived. There were a lot of their vehicles and their cars up there, and soldiers were moving from one room to another, and they were saying that we should pack up, that they were moving us. We all went into the cinema hall; that was the biggest room in the cinema building. We were all lined up. Red Cross workers were sitting at a table. They had lists in front of them, so as you would walk up to them you would show them your card that you had received from them, and then they would ask you where you wanted to go: did you want to go to Travnik -- they were offering Travnik, Zenica, Stari Vitez, Kruscica; and also they would let you go to your home if you wished to. I chose to go home, because there was nowhere else for me to go. I thought that bygones should be bygones and that all things would end well after all. I walked home to Rijeka; I did not have any problems along the way. I saw that a few Muslim houses had been burned down in that area. When I arrived home, I saw what the situation was. The house was full of people who were driven out of their own homes, and that was the only accommodation they could get, in our house. They were all happy when I arrived, but when they started telling me about the things that were happening I realised that things were not good. They would not dare leave the house; they would eat the food they had in the house. Sometimes they would ask a soldier, an HVO soldier, to buy something for them and they would give him money, so there were such cases. I was very ill then; I was physically exhausted. I was upset and nervous while I was detained. I simply did not feel strong enough to walk any more so I lay in bed at home, I did not even go out. Our lady neighbour, a Muslim who worked in the health centre in Vitez, when she saw the condition I was in, she examined me and she gave me some pills and some injections, and she said that I should leave, because she had heard throughout Vitez that all the people who were released and who were allowed to go back to their homes were being rallied again, and up there in the Vitez -- in the health centre, she got some kind of paper for me, a paper saying that I was supposed to go to Travnik at the hospital there. So I left there in an ambulance from the health centre in Vitez. There was a member of the Red Cross there too, and a woman, a Croat who was pregnant, and who had to be taken to Travnik urgently to deliver her baby there, so we arrived in Travnik together. They put me in the hospital immediately. Medical checkups were made and I was sent to the ward for chest patients and I spent a lot of time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can interrupt, Mr. Beso. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would just like to ask Mr. Beso a small precision. He mentioned just a few minutes ago that one morning he noticed that prominent Muslims were all taken away. Was that by the Red Cross or were they taken away by the HVO? Prominent Muslims, you said, professors, people of high calibre were taken away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. No, later on I found out that the HVO had taken them away. I heard about that later when I was released from prison. They were taken to Kaonik, Busovaca. They spent some time there and afterwards they were released too, but they were not there while we were being registered by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to them afterwards? Were they taken by the Red Cross after that or did they go back home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, going back to the hospital, approximately how much time did you spend in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the hospital for about a month and a half or two months. Conditions were very difficult at the hospital. There was a shortage of medicine and a shortage of food, and I kept wondering about my grandmother and my mother. I did not know what had happened to them. I knew that all the other women who were staying with us were young and they could leave easily. I did not have anyone to ask. The phonelines were not operating. I did not see anyone. I decided to go to the village of Kruscica near Vitez. That is where my brother was and I thought that perhaps he might have some information, but he did not know anything either. Radio amateurs helped us get in touch with them -- rather we contacted our relatives in Zenica, but they did not have any information about my mother, and grandmother either. Later, when the cease-fire was signed, we found out that they were in Rijeka all the time, but towards the end of the war my grandmother, who was disabled, had died a natural death. The Red Cross buried her in the village of Gacice near Vitez. From that moment onwards, my mother continued to live there. When the cease-fire was signed, it was the holiday of Bajram, and there was more freedom of movement then. There were checkpoints on the roads, too; she took a bus and she went to visit and she never went back home. She spent some time in Stari Vitez after that. It was held by the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and then she came to Kruscica to stay with us. She told us what it was like for her down there in Rijeka, that she was hiding in the house all the time, that she would not go out. A Croat, a neighbour, took the cow away. He slaughtered it. His brother moved into our house at the insistence of my mother, together with his wife and children. From that moment on, she was helped by these people who were staying at our house. They took care of the food, because she is sick too, she is a heart patient, and they got medicine for her which was very expensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, when you got back to your house you said that there were many relatives that were in your house that had been expelled from their houses in the Rijeka area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were mostly women and children, because all the men were imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did the HVO expel these women from those homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were expelled from their homes by people, Croats, who would come from Zenica, who did not have any place to stay. They were expelled from their homes and they would simply move in, so they would simply allow them to take a few basic things, a bag with their personal belongings. They would not allow them to take anything else with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What happened to the women who were expelled from their homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly. I only know that in these few houses of ours and of our relatives, they stayed there, and later on, they went across HVO and BH-Army lines there in Vitez towards Zenica and they continued living in refugee camps there. They went on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, if we could just go back to the previous photograph, which is exhibit 56, it is underneath the photograph that is on the easel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, perhaps I will take advantage of this minute to have another clarification. Mr. Beso, you said that your mother invited your Croat neighbours to come and live with you; is that right? Were these neighbours Croat who came and helped her and gave her medicine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the relationship between Croat neighbours and Muslim neighbours were good relations, or did she do that for protection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She did that to protect herself. That is why it was done, because the people in Rijeka, some Croats were willing to help, others were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you felt safe when this Croat family came and lived with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not me, I was not there at the time, I was in hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just meant your family. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the court's permission, Mr. Beso, if you could stand up once again at exhibit 56, and if you could use the pointer and point to the area that you described as Krcevine. I believe this is 56B?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the village of Krcevine (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is the exact place where you were digging trenches off the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot really find my way on this map, but it is a little bit removed from the village of Krcevine where the line was formed. I was digging trenches outside the village. There was some kind of a building, something like a chapel there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, once again if I could ask the usher to place this map; it can go right on top of those two. This is a copy of exhibit 29. I believe at this point this will be 29F, if I am not mistaken, Mme Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is 29F.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, while this map is going up, may I approach?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It is for the witness to show us where he dug trenches; is that so, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We are going to use this map to depict on this map exactly where he dug the trenches and that will conclude the examination. Once again, using the orange marker, Mr. Beso, could you mark the three areas or circle the three areas on this map where you dug trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village of Krcevine, the village of Ciganluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You call it Sofa as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You have marked it with three Roman numerals, your Honour, I, II and III. Where else on this map were you told people were digging trenches, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village of Jardol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is fine. Where else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We called it Crveno Brdce, near the village of Vraniska. Kuber. I do not know exactly where the lines were, I was not there. When I was in the cinema, the prisoners said that they went near the stadium; in the direction of Stari Vitez, there were dugouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you mark those as well? Did you also mention a village called Krcevine Kuce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a village known as Krizancevo Selo. Then there are a few houses where the Krisance live, and we call that Crveno Brdce, the red hill. It is near Dubravica, I cannot seem to be able to find it on the map. Here somewhere (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The mark you have put is the approximate area near Dubravica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, near Dubravica. I do not know exactly where the lines were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Any other areas that you heard of, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you. You can have a seat, sir. Mr. Beso, when you went back to your brother's house in Kruscica after your stay in the hospital, did there come a time when you rejoined the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you continue to be in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am a professional soldier of the army of the Federation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What rank do you hold in that army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no rank; I am just a soldier, a private.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I might have one moment to consult with my colleagues? (Pause). Your Honour, at this time I have no further questions of Mr. Beso other than I would like to admit into evidence Prosecutor's exhibit 29F, 50B and 56B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see there are no objections on the part of the Defence. In that case, I think that Defence can continue with its cross-examination. Mr. Beso, before you answer those questions, I think the Prosecutor probably told you -- can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before you answer questions put to you by Mr. Nobilo, I suppose that the Prosecutor has told you you are a witness for the Prosecution, you are appearing before a court, you have a man who has been accused of grave crimes, he needs to be defended, and you will now be subjected to questions put to you by the Defence lawyer or lawyers. After that, possibly additional questions will be put to you by the Prosecution again, whose witness you are. There always may be a couple of questions put to you by the judges. Mr. Nobilo, you have the floor until roughly 1.00 pm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Beso, good day. I am Anto Nobilo, Defence counsel for General Blaskic. Can you tell me when the people in Bosnia-Herzegovina started en masse to refuse to join the JNA? Could you give us a date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when the war in Slovenia and Croatia started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You worked in a mechanics repair shop in the JNA; can we call it a logistics service? What about the other people who were working in logistics like cooks, warehouse, guards and others? Did they undergo the same training as you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, I had the training as I just described it. Of course, they also had specialised training as cooks, quartermasters, bakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, but I am asking about the infantry training, the short infantry training.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know that President Izetbegovic had proclaimed a general mobilisation in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General mobilisation? Believe me, I do not know exactly. You see, I did not engage in politics at all and I did not watch television.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But the question of young men joining the army, did they do so on a voluntary basis or were people simply mobilised to join?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mostly on a voluntary basis, because when it was seen what was happening in Croatia and this was shown by BH television, then, of course, the impressions changed. We all knew that the JNA had withdrawn from Slovenia almost entirely to Bosnia, so we knew something would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, but you in Vitez or you personally, were you called up by the defence department, or did you go on your own initiative some place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did get a call-up once. At first I refused and then later on I joined voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But at first, you were called up. Tell me, what about your colleagues, neighbours, Muslims? I am thinking of the Muslims. Were they also called up; did they also join the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended. Some did, some did not. Some went of their own free will, some left Vitez, went abroad; it depended on the personal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know what was the age for admission to the BH-Army, the minimum and the maximum age limit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main prerequisite was people who had completed their service in the JNA. Later, if you were of age also you could join the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the upper age limit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You were called up by whom, the first call-up papers? Who sent them to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received this call-up from the Defence Secretariat in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, I do not know the date or the period. It must have been when there were some problems around Bosanski Brod. It was then, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was that in 1992, 1993 or 1991? Can you at least tell us the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in 1992, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where were the officers of the National Defence Secretariat in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the municipality building of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you joined voluntarily the second time, where did you report to, which building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I reported to the building in Stari Vitez. It was the fire brigade building there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When was that; do you remember the year at least?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was it the end of 1992 or earlier? Was it winter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the autumn, beginning of winter. I do not know, I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you joined, which unit did you join? We heard that you guarded the relay station, but which unit did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How can I explain that to you? I was not in any particular unit, I was simply assigned to that position to secure the relay station. I do not know exactly how many men there were. There were some younger people, some older ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And your brother, did he join the BH-Army voluntarily or was he called up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He went voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What unit did he join?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an infantry unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where was the command accommodated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In old Vitez. For a time there was a kind of regional headquarters in the village of Novaci near the impregnacija in an office of the Motoring Society of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And where was your command? Where was your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In old Vitez, and alternatively Stari Vitez and Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But where did you report? Did you report to somebody who gave you assignments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, when I came to Stari Vitez, I was told what to do. My duty was simply to go to the relay station from my house. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you have a commander, a superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three or four of us per shift, so we did not need a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And who determined who would take which shift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly; we would make our own arrangements depending on our free time, when we were available. That is how we did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And when you agreed on something, did you report that to somebody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was just important that somebody should be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you have a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you have weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had a pistol, 9 millimetre pistol, with a regular licence issued by the SUP in Vitez long before the war. It was left to me by a relative who left for Switzerland and when I was captured, when they searched my house, an HVO member, Rajko Matkovic, took it away from me. I showed him the licence but he seized it nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And your comrades who secured the relay station with you, did they wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, maybe some of them had trousers, but we did not really have uniforms or weapons, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about at the relay station? Did anyone have a rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a Russian automatic rifle. We called it the PPS, so it was there, it was always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did HVO units ever secure the relay station or was it only the BH-Army that secured it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The relay station was built, I think, in 1986 or 1987, because we were in a kind of valley; we were surrounded by hills, so the reception was not good, particularly in the village of Kruscica, and so I think she self-financed its construction and BH television, Sarajevo studio in those days, helped to finance it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, but during the war did the HVO secure the relay station at all or only the BH-Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe that the HVO secured it, because it was in a Muslim village, so the HVO did not come there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Which was the village close to the relay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the villages of Kruscica and Vraniska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In Kruscica, when you went to the relay station, did you pass through Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I went through Rijeka, and there was a short cut, so it was much closer that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In Kruscica, were you ever near the Lovac motel in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had a girlfriend from Kruscica and we used to walk there often.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see the HVO in the Lovac motel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were in the Lovac motel, in the Ribnjak -- it was called the Ribnjak in those days and the Lovac motel, yes, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know who was accommodated in 1992 in the Lovac motel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was it a headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. There were vehicles there and troops, but what it was I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, where were you on 15th April 1993? The 16th the shooting started, but the day before, where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at my girlfriend's. We spent a lot of time together. I was in her house in Kruscica. I stayed quite late, it was dark, I did not know anything, and in the evening, about 10.00 or 10.30, I was going alone along the road from Kruscica to my house. It took maybe ten minutes on foot and I did not notice anything, only close to my house, I met two neighbours, Croats, but they were not in uniform, they were in civilian clothes. We just said "good evening" to each other and that is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And the day before that where were you, on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the 15th you were with your girlfriend, but the day before where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly I was at the relay station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, the 14th or 15th, did you see any convoy of trucks, any large group of soldiers, 100, 200, 300, HVO troops passing by or rallying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, the situation was extremely tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But can you please answer my question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. Mr. Nobilo has asked a question and when the witness was answering the question, Mr. Nobilo broke in with another question. I simply ask Mr. Nobilo to allow the witness to finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Objection sustained. Mr. Nobilo, please give the witness time to finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
