utterances.text: Mr. President, you know I hear the answer faster than you, faster than the rest of the people in the courtroom. The witness started answering something else, so I begged him to answer my question first. My intention was not to interrupt him. Let me repeat. My question was: on 14th or 15th April, did you see any convoy of trucks with HVO troops or infantry troops, 100, 200 or 300?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but my answer may be a bit longer. I did not see a column of vehicles or a column of soldiers, but the situation in Vitez in those days was extremely tense, and if you went to the part of Vitez where the cinema was, where the MUP was, there were soldiers there always. HVO soldiers were always there, also near the marketplace, near the health centre and non-stop they would pass by my house in a car going to Kruscica where they stayed in the hotels.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But on the 14th and 15th, did you see a large group of troops or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that there was tension in the air. How could you feel this tension? How did you register this tension? On what grounds could you describe in more concrete terms this tension? What did it stem from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I need a little more time to answer this question. In Vitez, as everywhere else, one goes out in the evening, one goes to cafes. Quite a large number of Muslim cafes had been destroyed. Explosive devices were planted there in the evening, and for a time the use of the Bosnian dinar was prohibited in the marketplace, so that all these events contributed to people staying home or to more troops walking around town. That is the tension I refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In Rijeka, was any Croat cafe blown up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Rijeka? I think one was hit, but it did not -- it was not blown up, it continued working. I cannot remember exactly when that happened and who did it. I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What do you mean, "it was hit"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was hit with a projectile. What weapon was used I really do not know. I did not pass there often because I went towards Vitez passing by Sumarija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But the owner of the cafe was a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but this is just one case, whereas almost all the Muslim owned cafes in Vitez, nothing was left of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Apart from these cafes and bars in Vitez which were blown up, what about relationships among neighbours? Was there any harassment or mistreatment by your neighbours in Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no violence, only some people when you said hello to them, they would turn their heads away, but I am not really aware of any violence. Everybody was afraid. There were people with faces masked that would come into houses and loot them, but this did not happen in our village in Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you were arrested and later registered by the Red Cross, how did you register, as a soldier or as a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not even ask us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: They did not ask you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, just they asked you for your name and they give you a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But you were wearing civilian clothes and nobody asked you whether you were a civilian or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not, or at least I do not remember. I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Among the civilians who were with you in captivity, what age were the men; can you remember the age group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, at the beginning, there were prisoners from 16 and I cannot remember the upper age limit. This lasted for some time and then all those who were under age and who were sick were released home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You cannot remember how many days you spent in the veterinary station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, perhaps we can take advantage of your quest for your next question to stop here. We will resume work at 2.30. (1.00 pm) (Adjourned until 2.30 pm) 25 (2.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Madam Registrar, please bring in the accused. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please sit down, we shall now continue. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, when you finished your treatment at the Travnik hospital -- actually, can you tell me, during your treatment, under whose control was this hospital, or rather the ward where you were? Which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no army there at all; this was the hospital in Travnik. Actually both the BH-Army and the HVO were then in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In which part of Travnik was the hospital, where the HVO was or where the army was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time they were together in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you went from Travnik, I think you said you went to see your brother in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How did you get there, by car, on foot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went through forests; it was a long way to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is to say on foot, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I walked for two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Under whose control was that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army of the BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you came to Kruscica, under whose control was Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also the army of the BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I kindly request that we look at one of the maps. I know that the witness said he was digging trenches, so I am not going to ask him about those places, but I want to expand a bit on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, you spoke about trenches --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I hate to interrupt, but I thought counsel was going to tell us what we are putting on the board up here. I suspect before we start talking about it we should identify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think Mr. Nobilo said this was a map we would be looking at. However if you could truly identify this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Zenica 4, which includes the area of Vitez, the Yugoslav People's Army produced this map 1 to 50,000. This is a standard army map that was used in the former Yugoslavia, the same as the ones we have been using so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I just take a look at the map, your Honour, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Kehoe, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My only request with regard to the use of this map at any time this map has been used, and it is in the record on numerous other occasions, the map is wrong with regard to this city up in the upper left-hand corner which is known as Han Bila; that is what it is listed as. One of the other maps had a Bila up here. I stand corrected, this one is in fact correct. I am sorry. If I could stand up here Mr. President while this goes on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, if you so wish, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, when you were first digging trenches -- could you please get up, sir? Which places were held by the HVO; which positions were held by the HVO? So the first time when you went to dig trenches -- could you please get up and show this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you went to dig trenches the first time, what was the position of the HVO army? Which positions were held by the HVO en route to the place where you were digging trenches and in the place where you were digging trenches. Could you please show that to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Vitez somewhere around here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You are now showing HVO positions, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I showed it the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am going to mark HVO positions with a blue pen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, so there should be no ambiguity, your question was to give the positions of the HVO. We do not know whether the witness is a military expert to be able to give you those positions. He answered by saying that he dug trenches. So was your question the military positions of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, whether military positions of the HVO were where he was digging trenches. That was my question. Tell me, the positions of the BH-Army, did you see them as opposed to this, what the BH-Army held near the place where you were digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were then in the village of Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you indicate the village of Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you mark it this way? The second time you went to dig trenches, can you show us the place where you went to dig trenches then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So I am marking BH-Army positions with a red marker as the witness indicates it and I am showing HVO positions with a blue marker. So who held Pirici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pirici used to be a Muslim village and later they were held by the HVO when I came there to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The trench that you were digging and the positions that were held by HVO near Pirici, which village did it face; where was the BH-Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Poculice, Vrhovine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you show the positions of the HVO that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Above the village of Pirici, I do not know exactly where.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: From the position where you were digging trenches, could you see the positions of the BH-Army? Could you see the soldiers of the BH-Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, how could you see them? The HVO soldiers were hiding and the BH-Army soldiers were hiding and we were like a zone in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you or did you know where BH-Army soldiers were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A member of the HVO explained it to us; just by his hands he was showing us where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What did he say? At what distance were the BH-Army soldiers from the place where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not speaking in terms of metres. He was just saying approximately that they were there in that forest, that they are here or there, near this house or that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How far away was that house and how far away was that forest from the place where you were standing and in what direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not familiar with the terrain. I just know the village here, Pirici, Ahmici, Sivrino Selo and then Poculica, Vrhovine and further on towards Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who held Poculica and Vrhovine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who held Sivrino Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you indicate Sivrino Selo to me? So we are going to circle it this way, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Poculica? When you went to dig trenches for the third time, could you indicate the positions of the HVO to me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village of Krcevine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was the village of Krcevine held by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was its position immediately at the very first point in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Further up towards Bocko, Tolovici, Ljubic. I do not know, I do not know the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we indicate the HVO army positions here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who held Tolovici, can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you show Tolovici? Tell me, above Krcevine, where was the BH-Army to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where were the closest positions of the BH-Army in relation to Krcevine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So this was the third time that you were digging trenches. Did you hold any other positions -- did you go to dig trenches elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not go anywhere else, although I heard that there were some groups that went to other places as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now these groups that you heard about, did they tell you where the BH-Army was and where the HVO was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody knew it at the time, because you could not see anything properly, only if you heard something from the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who held Kuber at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kuber?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure, but I know prisoners also went to dig trenches there. Where the lines were, whether they were here, I do not know exactly. They were nearby, near Kuber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So the BH-Army and the HVO had their lines in Kuber, right? Can we mark them? Where is Kuber; can you show it to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour, the witness just said he did not know where the lines were in Kuber and counsel then wants to mark lines on Kuber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is the President who is going to intervene. Mr. Beso, will you turn to face me. Do you consider yourself capable of answering the questions? Is it within your competence as a military man to answer the questions put to you by Mr. Nobilo? Will you tell me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really. I can show you where Kuber is, but I cannot really show you where the lines were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Nobilo, please proceed to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, when did you come to Kruscica from the hospital? Can you tell us when this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell me the month and year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps the beginning of August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So the beginning of August of 1993. Did you immediately join the BH-Army in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was spared for about two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you became a soldier for the BH-Army in Kruscica two months after you arrived there; this was in October?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the witness, what the witness is saying. The witness needs to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am repeating my question: is it true that in October 1993 you became a BH-Army soldier in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was before the conflict between the HVO and the BH-Army. That was October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now we are talking about 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, perhaps it would be more comfortable if you do not need the map any more, then the witness could speak from his seat if you do not need the map any more; it may be more comfortable for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But I will need him again after two or three questions by the map too. I asked you, after your return from the hospital, when did you become a soldier of the BH-Army again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the end of September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Then, as a soldier, were you aware of BH army positions in Kruscica and in the municipality of Vitez in general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, I was guarding the waterworks of Elicja. This is also in Kruscica, that is the water works supplying Vitez and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know which places were held by the BH-Army and which places were held by HVO after you became a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in the municipality of Vitez? The Armija was in part of Stari Vitez, the villages of Busovaca --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I will mark with a red X the places where the BH-Army was. Ljubic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Poculica, the village of Kruscica, Vranjska, Sanovaca, Poculica, Vrhovine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Only the villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know where the villages were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know any other places that the BH-Army held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tolovici, as we said; these other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I wish to indicate that the red pen is BH-Army. I wish to indicate that on the map, the red pen is the BH-Army and the blue pen is the HVO, and I should also like to mark 1993, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The position is indicated by the witness, of course, Mr. Nobilo, according to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, what the witness said was that he was asked to dig trenches at three different locations and he said that was in April/May 1993, and then counsel jumped ahead to October 1993, to go into positions in October 1993. That is quite different than what Mr. Nobilo wanted to put on this chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They are marked differently, your Honour, with crosses and some with lines. The map is absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman. Perhaps what would be simplest, Mr. Nobilo, is that you indicate on the map as you have done for each of your exhibits the dates to which these positions of the BH-Army and the HVO correspond with big letters and figures. Mr. Kehoe, would you like to approach the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, you were digging trenches some time in April 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Nobilo. The date, because that is what was disputed by the Prosecution. Can you indicate on the map as you have done on other occasions the month and the year to which these indications given by the witness apply. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is exactly what I intended to do, but I am just double-checking with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I apologise in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Therefore you were digging trenches in April 1993. You joined the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina when, in September, after your treatment in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The end of September 1993, perhaps even the beginning of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So we have put down October 1993 with an X, the BH-Army with red and the HVO is marked with a blue pen, and April 1993 BH army is red but with a line. Is this clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is that clear, Mr. Kehoe now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Once again, it is not clear, your Honour, and that is not what the witness testified to. What the witness testified to on the blue marks are the locations that he dug trenches at. That is quite different from saying this is the lines. That was what this witness said were the trench-digging locations, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, I am not at all in agreement with you, Mr. Kehoe. The Defence was very clear. He asked questions to the witness regarding the lines of the HVO, and of the BH-Army. In fact, I intervened and asked whether he was capable of answering those questions and we continued without any objections, so Mr. Nobilo continued. You can say what you like about it, but I think the situation is very clear. He was not in a position not to be able to answer those questions. For the last time, Mr. Beso, listen to me carefully without any fear. Does this map correspond correctly to the defence lines or the attack lines of each of the two armies as you were able to perceive them while digging trenches. Please, look at the map once again, take your time and tell us whether this fully corresponds to the positions of the Bosnian Army or of the HVO. Does it correspond to what you wish to reply to Mr. Nobilo's question? Please be at rest, this is simply for the purpose of clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is all right; it is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the witness has answered. You can now go on to your next question, Mr. Nobilo. You may sit down, Mr. Beso.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, you are a professional soldier. What purpose do trenches serve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What purpose does a trench serve? A trench serves the purpose of protection so that a soldier can be protected in a trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is a trench used for offensive military actions or for defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends. You can get ready in a trench to mount an offensive if you want. That can be your initial position, but naturally it is also used for defence purposes too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: As a rule, what are trenches used for in the army? What do they teach you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just as I said right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: All right, thank you. When the young man took you to the cinema hall, once you said that he said he was from Zagreb and on another occasion he said from Kotor Varos. What did he explain to you? Did he have orders to take you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not have any kind of contact. We did not talk at all. He just came; he picked us up. I do not know whether he had orders or not when we came into the cinema hall. I do not know what it looked like. We were taken over by a military policeman. This man left immediately and I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you hear about Kotor Varos, Kobojna, a unit of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that the first position where you were detained, you were fed by the leftovers of the food that the army had. I am interested in where you got these leftovers from, from the plates of the soldiers or from the pot where the dish was prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, from the pot, and also wherever we went to dig trenches we always got canned fish too, but naturally you do not get it to take it with you. They come when they think we are hungry so it was not regular meals that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you got food from the pot, does that mean that you were given the same food as the soldiers were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in certain places.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you came to Kruscica, when you became a soldier, what unit did you join?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was assigned to guard the Elicja waterworks; that was where I was a guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That was your duty, but what unit did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean "what unit"; what brigade or something?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, what unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 325th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were its headquarters, its command in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think so. The command of the brigade was not in Kruscica then; I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The 325th Brigade, how many battalions did it have; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, three or four; I do not know exactly. Perhaps after the war -- I do not know during the war, during the fighting between the army and the HVO, how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am asking you about the period when you were there in 1993, and how many soldiers did the 325th Brigade have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: As a soldier, you were not directly the member of the brigade but of a battalion; of what battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the 1st battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where was its command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many soldiers did your battalion have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. Most of these people were locals, from Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: As a soldier, you did not belong to the battalion but probably a unit that was smaller than the battalion, a company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the guard service, as I said already. I guarded the waterworks; the waterworks were far away in the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But were you the member of a company or the 1st battalion of the 325th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The people from Zenica, the Croats who were refugees and who expelled certain Muslims from their houses, did they come with their families with their wives and children to live there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. While I was there, there were only soldiers there and later on I think their families came in too, at least that was the situation in the case of a relative of mine. A soldier came and asked him whether he would give him his house and whether he could take over his house in Zenica and so they would take their respective families there, but this relative of mine did not agree upon it, only after he was expelled from the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You were from Rijeka. Was not Darko Kraljevic your neighbour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did he live far away from your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He lived nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, him and his brother and their parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is Darko Kraljevic who commanded Vitezovi; are we referring to the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, what do you know about Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Darko before the war. I knew him well; we lived nearby. He went to school with a relative of mine. We even went out together on some occasions. At the beginning of the war, I hardly ever saw him. Whenever I did, he was in uniform, a few times in Vitez by the hotel. At home, whenever I would see him, some soldiers were always there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What did you hear about these soldiers of theirs, this army of his?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know first of all that they were members of the HOS. That is the only thing I heard, and later, that they went out of the HOS and that they became Vitezovi, I do not know why. I heard about that, that HOS in Zenica had joined the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I do not know if that was the reason why they got out of HOS; I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic, was he violent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not towards me, no. When we met, we would say hello.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But what did you hear about him in relation to others? What kind of man was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. Few people saw him often, at least the people I had any contact with. They did not talk about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know anything more about this unit and about Darko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that they were some kind of intervention force. They were accommodated in Vitez; I do not exactly know which part of Vitez. I heard it said that when there was a conflict with the HVO, they were in a cafe in Vitez called the Banta.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to tender this map as evidence of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Mme Fauveau, what will be the number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: D48. Mr. Prosecutor, you have no specific objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have completed our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I turn to the Prosecution again. Do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Very, very briefly, your Honour. With regard to Darko Kraljevic, you were asked some questions by Defence counsel concerning Darko Kraljevic and you said you saw him in uniform by the hotel in Vitez. What hotel are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hotel in Vitez. It was called the Vitez hotel. It did not have any other special name. Vitez hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many times did you see him at the hotel Vitez? I am talking about Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not enter the hotel; I would see him nearby, in front of the hotel. I do not know exactly how often, but several times, not often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You explained, again in response to a question by Defence counsel concerning a relative of yours who was asked to exchange his house and refused and after he refused he was expelled; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That question has already been answered. There is no need to insist on it any longer. It has been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am just asking a follow-up question about where that location --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see, you were preparing a question. There is a question mark in the transcript. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, where was it that your relative was expelled when he refused to exchange his house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where was he living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was living in the neighbourhood, also in Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Near your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were asked some questions again by Defence counsel concerning the Red Cross, and whether you were asked by the Red Cross if you were a civilian or a soldier. Do you recall that question by Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were there civilians as well as soldiers being held in the cinema at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, only civilians. I do not know about soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe the map that Defence counsel put into evidence is D48; Mme Fauveau, is that correct, D48?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, D48.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you. You marked three locations on the map on the easel in response to questions by the Defence and you marked three locations that are marked in blue. Do you see those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Those are the three locations that you were at, digging trenches; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know every other place that the HVO troops were deployed in that area during the period of time that you were being held in custody both in the veterinary station and in the cinema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I might have one moment to consult with my colleagues. (Pause). Mr. President, we have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me check with my colleagues whether they have any questions. Yes, Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, I think if I heard you rightly you said that you were arrested when you went out of the shelter where you were hiding with your mother, I think, and your grandmother. On that date, were you a soldier in the BH-Army or not yet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was, but I was on leave at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were not armed; you did not participate in any fighting at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also said that some local Serbs served in the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them when I was digging trenches at Sofa. That is where they lived too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did also some Muslims join the HVO? Shall I repeat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is okay. No, I did not notice a single one, nor did I see a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You told us the event when Jusuf Ibrakovic tried to escape and you said they split his head and started killing him until he fell down. Then the Commander, Slavko Papic, suggested that they should kill someone else as an example to scare the others. Did they kill other people just to give an example or they did not do that; it was just words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were just threats. While I was there, there were no more such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also spoke of the death of Almir Gadjun, who was killed when you were digging trenches facing the village of Krcevine, is that right, in the forest? He was shot and then he died when he was carried to the hospital. Was that very close to the front, to the line of where there was exchange of fires? Did you continue after that still digging trenches or did you withdraw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the line was very close, close to where we were diggings the lines of the BH-Army and the HVO, and when all this happened with him, we went on digging and doing what we were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was anybody else killed after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in my group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In other groups that you know of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, I confess to being slow in following maps, so will you be patient with me and help me to follow the map on the easel, exhibit D48? I invite you first of all to look at the indications given for April 1993. You have already explained that you could not tell whether in April 1993 the HVO had other positions, or, if they had, you could not tell where those positions were. Look at the map and see if you agree with my own observation. There are three trench-digging positions which you have indicated for April 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were three locations where I was digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were more locations, and I do not know the exact places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. For April 1993, how many army positions have you indicated on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know about the positions where I was digging. Those are the three that I have indicated in blue ink, in blue marker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What about the ones in red, the red curved lines? What were they intended to indicate? Not the red crosses, the red curved lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were in my opinion the positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Whether they actually were there, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you count with me four or five of those lines? How many lines do you count like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are four lines, but this was in answer to one of the questions put to me by Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I know. Is the red dot intended also to indicate the position of the army in Stari Vitez in April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In April 1993, did the HVO hold a position in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In April 1993, did the HVO hold a position in Vitez, not in Stari Vitez, but in Vitez proper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When on April 16th the conflict started, we who were captured were actually used to inform about certain positions -- were used to form positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I see. I will not pursue that aspect. Let us turn to October 1993. On the map you have indicated with crosses the positions then occupied by the army. How many crosses have you marked? I count nine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was also in answer to a question by Mr. Nobilo. These are Muslim villages. They are all Muslim villages in the municipality of Vitez, so they are the ones I indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said they are villages. Were they positions occupied by the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know exactly, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In that same month, October 1993, did the HVO occupy any positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On that map, for October 1993, have you indicated any HVO positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know at the time where the HVO positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Should I understand you then to be saying that on that map, for October 1993, you have not indicated any HVO positions because you did not know where any such positions were; is that your position today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know where the positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So although on that map for October 1993 you have indicated nine positions for the army and no positions for the HVO, that did not necessarily mean that the HVO did not then occupy any positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO also had positions, only I do not know where. I mentioned here the villages in which the Muslims were in the majority within the Vitez municipality, and there were positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Beso, the Tribunal wishes to thank you. We know that this must have entailed a great deal of effort to revive all those memories. You can now return home, hopefully to find some tranquility and when you are seen out by the Registrar, we can have the next witness. Mr. Usher, will you please see the witness out. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, your Honours. Our next witness will be Mr. Sulejman Kavazovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Mark Harmon, before the witness comes in, you have indicated approximately, of course, that you will need about two and a half hours; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me, sir in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Before reading the statement, will you please give us your name and surname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Sulejman Kavazovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You are going to read the declaration given to you by the usher. Read it, please. SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kavazovic, you may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have been cited by the Prosecution within the framework of a trial against General Blaskic. You are before judges, so you can speak without apprehensions. It will first be the Prosecution that will be asking you questions, then the Defence. For the moment it is the Prosecution. Mr. Harmon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kavazovic, could you please state your age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 15th July 1969. I am 28 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Vrhovine, Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where is that in respect of the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is three kilometres from the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the direction of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, towards Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is your educational background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a traffic technician. This is completed secondary school level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did you go to high school and to grade school? Could you please inform the Trial Chamber of that information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed my secondary technical education at the Bosta Asta (?) People's University, as it was called, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before moving to Belgrade, when did you leave the municipality of Vitez to go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After you graduated from school in Belgrade, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I joined the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were your duties and responsibilities in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a squadron leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What type of a squadron was that, Mr. Kavazovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mountain infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After you completed your one-year service in the JNA, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Belgrade again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did you do in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in a company as the head of the rolling stock in a transport company.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you were in charge of trucks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Belgrade before you returned to the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 18th February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why did you leave Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I was going to be mobilised. I had permanent residence in Belgrade, and I expected to be mobilised as a reservist into the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I take it that is something you did not want to do so you left Belgrade and returned to the Vitez municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not want that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After you returned to the Vitez municipality, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a while, I stayed with my parents, for about ten or fifteen days. Then I volunteered into the headquarters of the Territorial Defence in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the time you joined the Territorial Defence in Vitez, did Bosnian Croats also join the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did not get a translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew 13 or 14 Croats who were with me in the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell me those Bosnian Croats by name, can you identify who joined the TO with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. The first was Anto Furundzija, the second Zlatko Nakic, another Vlatko Mladic, Stipo Zigonja, Zeljo Sajevic, Zeljo Vrebac. Number 8 was Dragan Calic; Dragan Matkovic was the ninth; Vladko Malic was the tenth. There was an eleventh one, surname Botic, I cannot recall his first name. I remember his surname was Botic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the Territorial Defence when you volunteered to join?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it is 3.40. I let you ask the first question regarding the basic identification elements. Perhaps it would be a good idea to have a break now until 4.00 pm. (3.40 pm) (A short break) (4.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Madam Registrar, please have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Kavazovic, who was the Commander of the Territorial Defence when you joined it after returning from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Commander of the Territorial Defence upon my return to Belgrade when I volunteered was Major Hakija Cengic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were your duties and responsibilities in the Territorial Defence after you joined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I joined the Territorial Defence, I did not have any special duties, I was a plain soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Later on, did you have specific duties and responsibilities in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the Commander's driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you later have additional duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 24th July, I was appointed as head of the transportation unit of the municipal Territorial Defence staff in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kavazovic, while you were living in Vitez, were you arrested by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I lived in Vitez, I was arrested by the HVO on three occasions. The first time --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please tell us about the first time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time, I was a civilian. I was not wearing a uniform, I did not even have anything. I was normally walking around town, and three HVO soldiers stood in front of me, all of a sudden, with Vlado Santic and they asked me to come with them to the hotel Vitez and I came with them to the Vitez hotel. We entered the building from the other side, not from the main entrance; that is to say we used a different entrance. We walked into a room where I was interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you about Vlado Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just a second, excuse me. When was that, exactly, when you were arrested as a civilian? Do you remember the date approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The date was 7th September, or 8th September, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned the name Vlado Santic. Did you know Vlado Santic before your arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Vlado Santic as a policeman in the Yugoslav Police before he joined the police force as a civilian before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the time he arrested you, was he a member of any particular unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a member of the HVO, but I do not know which particular unit. He was in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have exhibit 33 shown to the witness, I am going to refer to specific photographs in exhibit 33. If the usher could place those on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before you put this on the ELMO, perhaps the usher could also remove the previous exhibits which are on the easel and which we do not need any more, that is provided we do not need them any more. Please do it, Mr. Usher, so we do not lose any time and in the future please take care of these things during the break. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I am going to ask you to please place, from exhibit 33, photograph 205 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In the meantime can I ask? Do you know why you were arrested as a civilian? Did they give you any reason on 7th September 1992, or were they arresting people indiscriminately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know why I was arrested, but probably because I was a member of the Territorial Defence. That is the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, can you take a look at the photograph that is on the ELMO and identify that particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. This is the hotel Vitez. This is a picture of the hotel Vitez. I came in this way when I was arrested (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "this way", will you use the pointer please and indicate on the photograph the entrance where you were taken. Indicating for the record, your Honour, a door on the right-hand side of the photograph number 205. Thank you very much, Mr. Usher. I am finished with that exhibit, it can be removed and the ELMO can be turned off. Mr. Kavazovic, where were you taken in the hotel Vitez after you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I was arrested, I was taken to room number 1 in the Vitez hotel on the right-hand side on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was the hotel Vitez a military headquarters, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hotel Vitez was HVO headquarters. Which one I do not know. At any rate, civilians were not admitted into the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened after you went into this particular room? Would you just explain to the court what occurred to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to a room which only had a table in it, nothing else; no other furniture was there. I was interrogated there by Vlado Santic, why I was in the Territorial Defence, what the Territorial Defence intended to do further on and how many people there were in the Territorial Defence. I did not give any answers to these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long were you interrogated by Mr. Santic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the room for about four hours and he interrogated me perhaps for half an hour and then I was waiting for an exchange to be carried out, because my Territorial Defence headquarters found out through some civilians that I was taken away so they kept me there before my people from the Territorial Defence came to exchange someone for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you eventually released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Turning to your second arrest, Mr. Kavazovic, when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It occurred on 20th October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did that occur at the same time there were events occurring between the HVO and Muslims in the city of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it happened when the town of Travnik was blocked and when the HVO blocked the city of Travnik. Nobody could enter Travnik and in a certain way, this was the situation in Vitez too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you explain to the court first of all the events surrounding your arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day, on 20th October, I was coming back from Visoko. I was driving a van and I came to my command in Vitez, with my officers there, and on that occasion, I found out -- actually, as I was passing through Ahmici, I realised that houses were burning. I did not understand a thing', I did not know what was happening. Five houses were burning in Ahmici. I arrived in Vitez and I saw that there were many units throughout Vitez, that the city was blocked in a way, that there were many soldiers on corners. We were staying near the high school. When I entered the building, I realised that Territorial Defence members and civilians and Muslims in general did not have any freedom of movement any more. We were not allowed to move anywhere so in a way we were under siege by the HVO. We spent some four hours there until agreement was reached between the Territorial Defence and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, let me interrupt you. When you say you were staying there, where is "there"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were in Posdina, in a house where we were accommodated as the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have the usher, your Honour, place what is a copy of exhibit 45 on the easel and have it marked as an exhibit, I will ask the witness to identify locations on that photograph. I believe, your Honour, this will be Prosecutor's exhibit 45C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mme Fauveau, 45C?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that will be exhibit 45C.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, could you take a yellow pen, please, and could you mark the location on Prosecutor's exhibit 45C of two locations. The first is the location where you were and the second is the then headquarters of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can do that. Headquarters of the Territorial Defence were in the Srednjoskolski high school in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you just colour the whole building with a yellow pen, please, Mr. Kavazovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the high school where the command, the headquarters of the Territorial Defence were. This is where logistics were, in this building. I was here with four of my colleagues from work and this is where the Commander and six or seven other people were with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "I was here", you were in the logistics building of the Territorial Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The logistics centre, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please have a seat. Thank you. Could you continue on now with relating the events relating to your arrest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived in the logistics centre, this building, on the orders of Hakija Cengic, the then Commander, conditions were created for an agreement between the Army and the HVO for our safe departure from the command; that is to say that we could withdraw from the headquarters in the high school towards Mahala. The command was the first to move out, the Commander and the people with him left the building. They were allowed to leave and they went to Mahala to a private house, where they then stayed. Then the rest were supposed to leave. After that, when we talked to the commander, he ordered us to take out of our initial headquarters whatever we could and to put it in vehicles. We put it into the van, into the Golf and into the Fiat we had. We took the things that we managed to take with us and then we started moving towards Stari Vitez, towards Mahala. However, things were not as they were supposed to be. Between the hotel and the Vitez cinema, we were stopped by HVO members, 15 or more of them. They held RPGs. We were ordered to get out of the cars and we were arrested again. Omerdic Salih was with me in the same car, he was a communications officer and he and I were taken to the Vitez hotel again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the soldiers who arrested you include soldiers who had specific identifiable insignia on their shoulders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they all had HVO insignia. Two soldiers also had insignia saying that they belonged to the Ludvig Pavlovic unit. They took him to the terrace where Vlado Santic was who took me over and took me to that office again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did the insignia of the Ludvig Pavlovic brigade look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a leaf that looked like an oak leaf on it and underneath it said "Ludvig Pavlovic". To the best of my knowledge, people in Vitez were saying that this unit was from Herzegovina, that they were from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you wearing any insignia on any kind of a uniform that you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a uniform, I had a rifle and I had a pistol on my holster. When I was ordered to get out of the van -- I had taken my rifle and one of them showed me the sign "no" -- he pointed a RPG at me and I realised there was nothing I could do; I was forced to get out. On the left-hand side of my uniform, I had a sign showing that I was Territorial Defence. At that moment, one of these two people from the Ludvig Pavlovic unit tore off that patch off my uniform and he cursed, and he said, "What do you need this for? This will never be again", and he stepped on it. Then he grabbed my pistol, he tore it off, together with the holster and he took me to Vlado Santic, to the same stairway when I was first arrested. Then I was taken to another room, to room number 2 on the right-hand side this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were taken to the hotel Vitez a second time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see any kind of communications equipment in the possession of the soldiers who had arrested you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. These two had Motorolas, radio stations, these two members of the Ludvig Pavlovic unit, and also Vlado Santic had a Motorola.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is a Motorola?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Motorola is something used by the military and the police. It is used as communications equipment like a walkie-talkie. It is part of the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How far away from the hotel Vitez were you when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 15 metres away, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where was Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was waiting for me by the stairs. He stood there, arms akimbo, and then he took me to room number 2 together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who did he take you to room number 2 with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With those two members of the Ludvig Pavlovic unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Will you tell the court what happened after you entered that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I entered that room and I was ordered to sit down. I sat down. Then they had found some communications equipment, a radio, in the car and they asked me about that, what it was doing in my car and how come I had this. There were also two snipers that were not functional. You could not shoot with them; they did not have the optical equipment needed. These two snipers were from Zlemen, from the military warehouse which was blown up by the JNA, and that is how we had them; they were supposed to be prepared. So when I was driving this van, I got these snipers with the van without realising they were in there. Then they asked me how come I had this, where I was taking it and what the Territorial Defence intended to do if the HVO attacked. That is what they asked me about. They also asked me how many Mujahedin there were in Mahala and how many weapons there were in Mahala. I did not give any answer to all of that; I kept silent. One of them grabbed my shoulder with his hand and he said, "You will not be around for long." After this interrogation, I was taken to the hotel toilet, a floor underneath, and I was locked up into the women's toilet where water had flooded the floor and I had to stay there until 11.00 pm. Then after 11.00 pm, I was taken to the police headquarters of the HVO, the civilian police of the HVO. They put me in a room where there was no light, no electricity, no nothing. There was parquet on the floor and two blankets, two old dusty dilapidated blankets and also there was a toilet, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before I turn my attention to the MUP building and the conditions of detention in the MUP building, while you were in the bottom of the hotel Vitez, were there other Muslim prisoners in the basement or in the restroom area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was taken there, I was the first person to be taken there, together with Omerdic Salih, who was in the van together with me. We were the first two to be taken to the Vitez hotel toilet. Half an hour later, Patkovic Muhamed, Cazim Patkovic, and these other people who were with me in the Territorial Defence, they were also arrested. When they arrested me, they moved on to our building and they arrested them up there, and Mohammed Patkovic was physically abused. He was beaten up and then they brought him to where we were and we tried to help him out; we splashed him with water. He was bruised and it was difficult to talk to him because he felt faint and from that toilet, we were taken over to the police department, Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the police department, Mr. Kavazovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Briefly describe the conditions at the police kept.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions in the police department were non-existent. It was a room of two square metres. There was no furniture; there was only a window and a toilet. There was no water, there was no electricity, we were not allowed to ask for anything. Those were the basic conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When were you released from the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the morning of the fourth day I was exchanged and released. Agreement was reached when the fighting stopped in Novi Travnik. Agreement was reached to exchange prisoners, and on the morning of the fourth day, I was told that I would be exchanged for some other people who were arrested, and I was told that I would simply be released. Rabihic Nihad, a representative of my command, came and took me so I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You had been in the hotel Vitez on two occasions as a result of your arrest and you knew the hotel Vitez was a military headquarters. Let me ask you a couple of questions about the hotel Vitez, Mr. Kavazovic. First of all, you are a Muslim, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did Muslims have free access to the hotel Vitez when it was a military headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did HVO soldiers have free access to the hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you know him from your community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in the hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him three times at the hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately when, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him some time in June 1992. I saw him in July and in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You saw him going into the hotel Vitez or coming from the hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him getting into the hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Kavazovic, I would like to turn your attention to 15th April 1993, and, focusing your attention on that date, you were still living in Vitez, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in a private house owned by Resad Burak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you go to work that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 15th in the morning I went to work at 7.00 and I worked until 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After you finished your work, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I finished work at 3.10, I headed for my house where I was living. From Mahala I went in the direction of my house where I was living. Along the route, I noticed that the situation in town was unusual; there seemed to be no civilians. There were groups of the HVO of two to three soldiers in combat gear standing next to buildings, and I thought it was rather strange, so I concluded that the situation was not good; there were no civilians obviously. There were these groups of soldiers next to buildings. I reached the house I was living in, seeing that the situation was serious --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there for just a minute, Mr. Kavazovic. Could you please approach the large aerial image that is to your left, Prosecutor's exhibit 45C. Using a pink highlighter, will you please colour in the location of your house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My house was here (indicates). It was a private house I was living in, a private home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you put the number 1 next to that house, please? Okay. You can have a seat again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, after you returned to your house, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I checked to see whether my wife was there. However, my wife was with her parents at their apartment, so I went in the direction of my in-laws' apartment to see my wife and, passing through the park, I saw three or four groups of six to seven soldiers each running in the direction of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How were those soldiers dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in full combat gear; they had camouflage uniforms, helmets on their heads and automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you kindly approach Prosecutor's exhibit 45C once again, and with the pink pen do two things: first of all mark the location of the apartment building where your wife was staying, and then, secondly, would you please with the pink pen mark the direction that you took from your house to the apartment building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my house where I lived, so I arrived from Mahala in civilian clothes. I was not allowed to wear uniform. I had to go in civilian clothes because I was going through a part of the town that was under the control of the HVO, this route that I covered from my house to my in-laws' apartment, so I went in civilian clothes when I left work, because I was not allowed to wear uniform. I did not dare wear uniform because of fear from the HVO as I was living in a part of the town that was under the control of the HVO. This is where my in-laws lived (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you please take that pink pen and colour in the building where your in-laws lived and place the number 2 next to that building? Using the pointer, Mr. Kavazovic, could you please point to the park where you saw these groups of HVO soldiers running in the direction of the hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was moving from my house, through this park, and from this direction (indicates), from the centre of town. There were three or four groups of six to seven soldiers each running towards the hotel through the park. They were running through the park in the direction of the hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately what time of day was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about 3.50 or maybe 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Kavazovic, you do not know whether they were actually running to the hotel Vitez or to another part of the town of Vitez but in the direction of the hotel Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were running. Yes, that is true. They were running in the direction of hotel Vitez. I saw them here, they were running along here, so they were going towards the centre, the part where the hotel is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You can again have a seat. I am going to ask you to get up in a few minutes to make some additional marks on that diagram. After you arrived at your in-laws' apartment, did you find your wife there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I found my wife. She was staying with her father.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at the apartment building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I entered the building of my in-laws, my wife was there, and, entering the building, I saw that the situation was not at all good, that people were in their homes, that some people were walking in haste or running towards home. Wherever they happened to be, they were running home, and I asked my wife to go out with me for a walk to see what was happening and that is what I did. I went out with my wife and we made a tour. We walked round town, and while we were walking the town was quite empty; there were no civilians, no vehicles, nothing. Then I said to my wife that we should go back to my in-laws' because the situation was not at all good. I saw groups of people in front of buildings, soldiers, and seeing soldiers in combat gear I realised that something was wrong, so we went back to my in-laws and when we got there, then my father and mother-in-law had learned that the town was under blockade, that nobody could go in or out, that there was no movement of civilians, and then they proposed that all four of us head towards Mahala, that is the part of the town inhabited by Muslims. We headed for the door, and a colleague of mine came out and said, "Stop, you are not going anywhere. It is over now. The situation is not good at all. A war can break out any moment." I asked him why. He said he did not know but he told me to go back into the apartment and not to budge. In spite of this warning, I walked through the door, went down the steps. About five metres outside the building, I saw enormous numbers of HVO troops that had blocked everything. There were three or four soldiers more or less guarding every building so as to prevent anyone coming out or going in. The roads were blocked with garbage containers. At the entrance to Vitez, at a crossroads, there were two or three containers so that cars could not pass by, and having observed that I felt scared and I went back to my in-laws' apartment, and that is what I did. When I entered the apartment, my father-in-law asked me why I had done that, and I told him that I was interested to see what was happening, and he said, "You have nothing to enquire about. Everything is blocked, so we have to sit tight where we are."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, will you take a green highlighter, please, if there is one at the witness stand, and please approach Prosecutor's exhibit 45C again. With the green highlighter, please mark the direction that you and your wife walked through the town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I mark the circle that my wife and I made when we went out for a walk around town?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the circle we made when we went out for a walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please take your seat again, Mr. Kavazovic. Let me ask you a couple of questions before I move on to another topic.
